Note: In Heliopolitan theology, Shu is generated by Atum and forms the first divine pair with Tefnut.
In Heliopolitan theology, Tefnut is generated by Atum and forms the first divine pair with Shu.

Atum and Ra were combined as Atum-Ra, linking the Heliopolitan creator with the setting and renewing sun. This compound deity became an important model of Egyptian solar theology without making every later solar cult a direct offshoot of it.
The Memphite Theology presents Ptah's heart and tongue as bringing Atum and the other gods into being through thought and authoritative speech.
The Pyramid Texts preserve early surviving references to Atum as a self-generated creator, father of Shu and Tefnut, and source of the Heliopolitan divine genealogy.
The Book of Amduat associates Atum with the evening and nocturnal phase of the solar cycle, when the aged sun enters the underworld.
The Litany of Re includes Atum among the named forms and manifestations through which Re is understood.
The Shabaka Stone places Atum within Ptah's creative act, presenting him as brought into being through Ptah's heart and tongue.
Geb is the son of Shu and Tefnut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Nut is the daughter of Shu and Tefnut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Shu and Tefnut are the twin children of Atum and the paired powers of dry air and moisture.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Shu as the power who separates and supports sky and earth, enabling the deceased king's ascent among the gods.
In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, Shu supports the elevated sky-goddess Nut after Ra withdraws from human society.
Geb is the son of Tefnut and Shu in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Nut is the daughter of Tefnut and Shu in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Tefnut with Shu as part of the first divine generation and as a power of purification, life, and cosmic stability.
Ptah and Sekhmet form the principal divine couple of Memphis.
Nefertum is commonly presented as the son of Ptah and Sekhmet in the Memphite triad.
Ptah was combined with the Memphite necropolis god Sokar and the resurrected Osiris as Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, joining creation, burial, and regeneration in one funerary deity.
Centuries after Imhotep's lifetime, Memphite tradition deified him as a son of Ptah and integrated the historical sage into the local divine household.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Ptah as a divine craftsman who fashions, restores, and equips the king's body for renewed life.
The Shabaka Stone gives Ptah the central creative role: the gods and ordered world arise through his heart and tongue, understood as thought and speech.
Geb and Nut are sibling-consorts whose separation establishes earth and sky.
Osiris is one of the children of Nut and Geb in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Isis is one of the children of Nut and Geb in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Seth is one of the children of Nut and Geb in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Nephthys is one of the children of Nut and Geb in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
The Pyramid Texts repeatedly address Nut as the sky and divine mother who receives, protects, rebirths, and raises the deceased king.
Nut is the Heavenly Cow whose elevation creates the sky after Ra withdraws from humanity.
Osiris is the son of Geb and Nut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Isis is the daughter of Geb and Nut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Seth is the son of Geb and Nut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Nephthys is the daughter of Geb and Nut in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
The Pyramid Texts identify Geb as the earth-god, a source of royal inheritance, and father of the Osirian divine family.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow places Geb within the succession of divine rule and the reorganization of the cosmos after Ra's withdrawal.
In the Contendings of Horus and Seth, Geb acts as an elder divine authority who supports the settlement of the royal inheritance in favor of Horus.
Thoth and Maat represent complementary aspects of ordered knowledge: Maat is right order, while Thoth records, measures, articulates, and applies it in divine judgment and ritual.

Imhotep and Thoth became closely associated with learned, scribal, medical, and magical wisdom. Later tradition elevated Imhotep beside established gods of knowledge without making him simply an incarnation of Thoth.
The Pyramid Texts provide early surviving evidence for Thoth as divine scribe, ritual mediator, and participant in the settlement of conflicts among the gods.
The Book of Amduat places Thoth among the divine powers assisting the ordered nightly passage and renewal of the sun.
In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, Thoth serves Ra as adviser and is assigned authority over knowledge, administration, and the ordering of the divine realm.
The Shabaka Stone associates Thoth with the divine tongue and effective speech through which Ptah's thought becomes reality.
The Book of Two Ways invokes Thoth within the ritual knowledge and divine protection required to navigate the paths of the afterlife.
The Litany of Re includes Thoth within the solar liturgy and the ordered divine company surrounding Re.
The Hymn to Thoth directly praises him as lord of writing, reckoning, knowledge, ritual speech, and the measured order of time.
Hathor frequently appears as a daughter and Eye of Ra; some traditions also pair her with solar gods as a consort.
Hathor can appear as the mother of Horus, while other local traditions pair a Hathor-form with an adult Horus as consort.
Some local traditions name Hathor as Nefertum's mother, while the standard Memphite genealogy more often makes him the son of Ptah and Sekhmet.
Hathor and Mut were sometimes assimilated as royal mother-goddesses, especially in New Kingdom and later theology.
Hathor and Isis overlap as maternal, royal, protective, and funerary goddesses, leading to frequent later identifications.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow names Hathor as the Eye of Ra sent to punish rebellious humanity; her destructive aspect is also identified with Sekhmet.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Hathor as a maternal and funerary goddess who receives and supports the deceased king.
Sekhmet is a lioness-form of the Eye of Ra and is regularly described as his daughter.
Late temple theology could identify Isis with lioness and Eye-of-Ra forms that overlap with Sekhmet, although the two remained distinct deities.
Nefertum is commonly the son of Sekhmet and Ptah in the Memphite triad, though other maternal variants also occur.
Mut and Sekhmet were closely assimilated at Thebes, where Mut could assume a lioness form and Sekhmet's protective force.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Sekhmet as a powerful protective goddess whose force can strengthen and defend the king.
The Ebers Papyrus invokes Sekhmet and her priestly specialists within a medical-magical tradition that treats divine danger and healing as closely connected.
The Book of Amduat includes Sekhmet among the protective divine powers surrounding the sun's passage through the underworld.
The Litany of Re incorporates Sekhmet into solar theology as a fiery and protective manifestation of divine power.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow presents the Eye of Ra as Sekhmet during the near-destruction of humanity and as Hathor after her pacification.

Secondary Name: Calendars of Lucky and Unlucky Days
Note: The Calendars of Lucky and Unlucky Days connect particular days with myths and dangers involving Sekhmet, making her power relevant to everyday timing and conduct.
Maat is commonly called a daughter of Ra and accompanies his solar order; offering Maat to the gods symbolizes the king's maintenance of the order on which divine and human life depend.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Maat as right order and legitimacy, placing the king within the divine structure of justice and cosmic balance.
The Book of Amduat uses Maat as the standard of the ordered paths and processes that govern the sun's nocturnal passage.
Amun and Ra were combined as Amun-Ra, joining Amun's hidden creative power with the visible and renewing sun. The compound deity became central to New Kingdom state religion.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Ra as the solar ruler who receives, renews, and raises the deceased king within the celestial order.
The Book of Amduat is organized around Ra's twelve-hour journey through the underworld and his renewal at dawn.
The Litany of Re praises Re through a long sequence of named forms and manifestations used in royal funerary ritual.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow centers on Ra's rule, humanity's rebellion, divine punishment, and his withdrawal into the sky.
The Instruction of Amenemope invokes Re within its moral and theological language, placing human conduct under a divinely ordered cosmos.
Osiris and Isis are sibling-consorts and the parents of Horus in the central Osirian cycle.
Osiris and Seth are brothers whose conflict structures the myth of death, succession, and restored kingship.
Later traditions commonly present Anubis as a son of Osiris and Nephthys, although his parentage varies in earlier sources.
Osiris and Nephthys are siblings in the Heliopolitan genealogy.
Horus is the posthumous son and royal heir of Osiris in the Osirian cycle.
Theban theology could coordinate Amun-Ra with Osiris by presenting the solar god's visible life and the underworld god's bodily regeneration as complementary dimensions of one cosmic cycle.

The Pyramid Texts provide the earliest extensive surviving evidence for Osiris as ruler of the dead and model of the deceased king's restoration, although the complete later narrative is not told in one continuous account.
The Book of Two Ways locates the deceased within an Osirian underworld and supplies the knowledge required to reach protected divine regions.
The Litany of Re joins solar and Osirian theology by coordinating Re's nightly death and renewal with Osiris's regenerative body in the underworld.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris praises Osiris's kingship, restoration, afterlife authority, and the roles of Isis and Horus in preserving his rule.
In the Contendings of Horus and Seth, Osiris speaks from the underworld as Horus's father and presses the divine tribunal to recognize his son's inheritance.
The Great Hymn to Amun coordinates Amun-Ra with Osirian regeneration, presenting solar creation and underworld renewal as complementary divine powers.
The Shabaka Stone incorporates the conflict and reconciliation surrounding Osiris, Horus, and Seth into its Memphite account of divine order and kingship.
Isis and Seth are siblings in the Heliopolitan genealogy and opponents in the struggle over Horus's inheritance.
Isis protects and raises Anubis in some later traditions; his biological parentage is more often assigned to Osiris and Nephthys.
Isis and Nephthys are sisters who act together as mourners and protectors of Osiris.
Isis is the mother and protector of Horus in the Osirian cycle.
Isis and Mut overlap as royal mother-goddesses and were increasingly assimilated in New Kingdom and later temple theology, while retaining distinct cult identities.
The Pyramid Texts provide early surviving evidence for Isis as Osiris's sister-wife, mourner, protector, and mother of Horus.
The Book of Two Ways invokes Isis as a protector whose ritual power assists the deceased through the dangerous afterlife paths.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris praises Isis as the loyal sister-wife who protects Osiris, restores his authority, and secures the succession of Horus.
The Contendings of Horus and Seth presents Isis as Horus's forceful and resourceful advocate throughout the dispute over kingship.
The Great Hymn to Amun places Isis within a broader theology that coordinates Theban, solar, and Osirian divine powers.
The Pyramid Texts preserve Seth's characteristic ambiguity: he is implicated in the conflict with Osiris yet can also support, strengthen, or raise the king in other ritual settings.
The Book of Amduat includes Seth in his protective solar role, defending the sun-god against hostile forces during the night journey.
The Contendings of Horus and Seth makes Seth the rival claimant to kingship and subjects his conflict with Horus to prolonged divine litigation.
The Litany of Re includes Seth within the solar divine order, especially through his protective and forceful role in defending Re.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris identifies Seth as the hostile force behind Osiris's death and contrasts his violence with Osiris's restored rule.
The Shabaka Stone recounts the dispute between Horus and Seth and its settlement as part of the establishment of legitimate kingship and territorial order.

Secondary Name: Calendars of Lucky and Unlucky Days
Note: The Calendars of Lucky and Unlucky Days associate several dates with episodes involving Seth, making his disruptive and protective aspects part of ritual timekeeping.
Anubis is commonly presented in later tradition as the son of Nephthys, often by Osiris.
The Pyramid Texts provide early surviving evidence for Anubis as necropolis guardian, embalmer, and protector of the royal dead.
The Book of Two Ways invokes Anubis as a guardian and guide within the routes and gates of the afterlife.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris presents Anubis within the funerary care and protection surrounding Osiris's restored body.
The Pyramid Texts pair Nephthys with Isis as a mourner, protector, and helper in the restoration of the deceased king.
The Book of Two Ways invokes Nephthys with Isis as a protective funerary goddess assisting the deceased.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris places Nephthys beside Isis in the lamentation and protection of Osiris.
The Book of Amduat includes Nephthys among the divine powers participating in the sun's underworld renewal.

The Turin King List preserves the name Meni as the first human ruler after the divine dynasties. The later Meni/Menes tradition is often associated with Narmer, but that identification remains uncertain.
Horus could be coordinated with Amun-Ra in compound forms such as Amun-Ra-Horakhty, joining hidden creative power, the visible sun, and royal horizon symbolism.
The Pyramid Texts provide early surviving evidence for Horus as royal heir, opponent of Seth, avenger of Osiris, and divine identity of the living king.
The Book of Two Ways invokes Horus within the network of divine guardians and powers governing safe passage through the afterlife.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Great Hymn to Osiris presents Horus as the son who protects, vindicates, and succeeds Osiris.
The Book of Amduat includes Horus among the divine protectors and agents of solar and Osirian renewal.
The Litany of Re includes Horus in solarized forms, especially Horakhty, within its catalogue of Re's manifestations.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow places Horus within the divine order reorganized after Ra's withdrawal from earth.

Imhotep served Djoser as a high official and is traditionally associated with the design of the Step Pyramid complex. His later reputation as architect, sage, and healer greatly expanded beyond the limited contemporary evidence.
The Turin King List includes Djoser within the Third Dynasty sequence and preserves his place in later Egyptian royal chronology.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Nefertum as the lotus-born fragrance of the rising sun, connecting him with renewal and rebirth.
Amun and Mut form the divine couple at the center of the Theban triad.
Khonsu is the son of Amun and Mut in the standard Theban triad.
The Great Hymn to Amun gives an extensive theological portrait of Amun as hidden creator, solar power, universal ruler, and protector of worshippers.
Amun appears in portions and versions of the Book of the Dead, often in solar hymns or protective invocations; the corpus does not present one uniform doctrine of Amun.
The Book of Amduat includes Amun among the divine powers incorporated into the nightly solar journey, although Re remains the text's central figure.
The Instruction of Amenemope invokes Amun as a protector and moral authority, especially in its concern for restraint, humility, and the vulnerable.
The Teaching of King Amenemhat I is addressed to the king's son and successor, Senusret I, and frames succession through vigilance, royal duty, and inherited authority.
The Tale of Sinuhe is set during the death of Amenemhat I and the accession of Senusret I, who later summons Sinuhe home and restores him to royal favor.
The Turin King List preserves Senusret I's place in the Twelfth Dynasty sequence.
The Turin King List preserves Senusret III's place in the Twelfth Dynasty sequence.
Khonsu is the son of Mut and Amun in the standard Theban triad.
Mut appears in Book of the Dead traditions as a protective mother-goddess and member of the wider divine company invoked for the deceased.
The Coffin Texts contain early references to Khonsu, including his lunar movement and his power over time, protection, and the fate of the deceased.
The Book of Amduat includes Khonsu among the gods accompanying and assisting the solar passage through the Duat.
The Litany of Re includes Khonsu within the divine company and solarized forms surrounding Re.
The Great Hymn to Amun situates Khonsu within the Theban divine household of Amun and Mut.
Miriam and Aaron are siblings in the biblical Exodus tradition.
Miriam and Moses are siblings in the biblical Exodus tradition.
Aaron and Moses are brothers in the biblical Exodus tradition.
Akhenaten and Nefertiti were the central royal couple of the Amarna court and Aten cult.
Tutankhamun is generally identified as a son of Akhenaten, although the surviving evidence does not preserve a simple contemporary statement of the relationship.

Secondary Name: The Great Hymn to the Aten
Note: The Great Hymn to the Aten is a central expression of the royal theology promoted under Akhenaten. It names Akhenaten as the Aten's unique royal intermediary, but the surviving inscription does not securely identify him as its personal author.
The Poem of Pentaur centers on Ramesses II's conduct at the Battle of Kadesh and repeatedly praises him through his royal names and titles.
Egyptian creation traditions describe Atum emerging from Nun, the undifferentiated primeval waters, to initiate the ordered world.
Solar creation traditions place the first appearance of the sun-god against the background of Nun's primeval waters; the exact genealogy varies among theological centers.
Nun represents the undifferentiated pre-cosmic state, while Maat represents the ordered and sustainable structure established within creation.
The Pyramid Texts invoke Nun as the primeval waters from which the creator and the renewed king can emerge.
The Book of Amduat places the solar journey within the primeval waters of Nun, from which the renewed sun emerges.
The Book of the Heavenly Cow invokes Nun as the ancient pre-creative background against which the divine world is reorganized.

The Aten began as the visible solar disk within older Re-centered theology. Under Akhenaten, it was elevated into the exclusive focus of the royal cult rather than simply replacing Re without continuity.

Secondary Name: The Great Hymn to the Aten
Note: The Great Hymn to the Aten is the fullest surviving exposition of the Aten as universal source of light, life, fertility, time, and royal authority.
The Instruction of Hardjedef and the Instruction of Kagemni belong to the Egyptian sebayt tradition and share concise advice on restraint, household conduct, and elite self-discipline.
The Westcar Papyrus presents Djedefhor, or Hardjedef, as a learned prince at Khufu's court, reinforcing his later literary reputation as a sage.
The Instruction of Kagemni and the Instruction of Ptahhotep are preserved together in Papyrus Prisse, giving them a direct manuscript association within the sebayt tradition.
The Coffin Texts reuse, adapt, and expand many Pyramid Text utterances while extending funerary access beyond the exclusively royal setting of the Old Kingdom corpus.
The Instruction of Merikare and the Instruction of Ptahhotep belong to the sebayt tradition, but apply its ethical language to different settings: royal governance and elite personal conduct.

The Kahun medical texts and the Edwin Smith Papyrus belong to Egyptian scribal medicine, although the former emphasizes gynecology and veterinary material while the latter is especially associated with trauma and surgery.
The Teaching of King Amenemhat I and the Instruction of Merikare are royal instructions that use admonition, memory, and ethical kingship to guide a ruler or successor.
The Coffin Texts preserve and expand offering formulas, mortuary recitations, and Osirian ritual material also represented by the Abydos funerary liturgy.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Abydos funerary liturgy and the Great Hymn to Osiris share the cult of Osiris at Abydos, emphasizing offerings, restoration, royal afterlife, and sacred memory.
The Book of Two Ways is a distinct group of underworld maps and spells preserved within the larger Coffin Texts corpus.

The Prophecy of Neferti predicts the rise of a southern king named Ameny, most plausibly Amenemhat I, while the Teaching of King Amenemhat I presents that dynasty's royal voice and succession ideology.

The Prophecy of Neferti and the Admonitions of Ipuwer both use images of social inversion, foreign threat, and the collapse of order, although they are separate literary compositions with different purposes.
The Teaching of King Amenemhat I and the Loyalist Instruction belong to the royal sebayt tradition and emphasize loyalty, vigilance, hierarchy, and service to the king.

Secondary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Hymn to the Nile and the Great Hymn to Osiris share a theology of fertility, agricultural renewal, and restored life, without implying that one text directly borrowed from the other.
The Book of the Dead inherits and adapts many Coffin Text spells, reorganizing Middle Kingdom funerary material into a long-lived New Kingdom and later corpus.
The Loyalist Instruction and the Instruction of Amenemope continue the sebayt tradition, linking ethical conduct with social order, restraint, and proper relations to authority.
The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus and Berlin Papyrus 6619 preserve related Middle Kingdom scribal mathematics, including practical numerical and geometric problem solving.
The Kahun and Ebers papyri belong to the Egyptian medical scribal tradition and combine observation, diagnosis, remedies, and ritual-magical practice.

Primary Name: Great Hymn to Osiris (Stela of Amenmose)
Note: The Book of the Dead develops the Osirian themes praised in the Great Hymn to Osiris, including justification, bodily restoration, protection, and renewed life under Osiris's authority.
The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus and Berlin Papyrus 6619 preserve related Egyptian computational traditions, including arithmetic procedures and algebraic-style problems.
The Book of Gates follows the Amduat within the New Kingdom tradition of royal underworld books, mapping the sun's nightly passage through ordered regions of the Duat.

Primary Name: The Great Hymn to the Aten
Note: The Great Hymn to the Aten and the Great Hymn to Amun both praise a universal solar creator, but the Aten hymn systematically excludes other gods while the Amun hymn integrates many divine forms into Amun's hidden unity.

The Book of the Heavenly Cow and the Book of the Earth both organize the cosmos through divine bodies and the separation or interaction of sky, earth, and underworld, though they belong to different mythic and funerary settings.

Primary Name: The Great Hymn to the Aten
Note: The Great Hymn to the Aten and the Hymn to Thoth share the formal language of divine praise and cosmic ordering, while presenting very different gods, institutions, and theological priorities.

The Book of the Earth continues the New Kingdom underworld-book tradition represented by the Book of Gates, but emphasizes the earth-god's realm, Osiris's hidden body, and solar regeneration rather than an hourly gate sequence.
The Decree of Horemheb and Necho II's Decree at Kusae are royal legal-administrative proclamations that regulate officials or temple interests and present the king as guarantor of order.
The Poem of Pentaur and the Victory Stela of Merneptah are royal monuments that transform military campaigns into declarations of divine favor, legitimate kingship, and state power.
The Book of the Earth and the Book of Caverns are closely related late New Kingdom underworld books centered on hidden regions of the Duat, Osiris's body, punishment, and solar regeneration.

The Tale of the Two Brothers and the Contendings of Horus and Seth use divine or semi-divine family conflict, injury, sexual rivalry, judgment, and restored status, but they are distinct narratives rather than direct versions of one another.
The Maxims of Ani and the Instruction of Amenemope belong to the late sebayt tradition and share practical advice on restraint, speech, household conduct, humility, and dependence on divine order.
Akhenaten transformed the pre-existing Aten into the exclusive focus of royal worship and made the king the principal intermediary between the solar disk and humanity.
Nefertiti appears with Akhenaten as a principal royal participant in Aten worship, receiving the Aten's rays and performing ritual roles normally centered on the king.

Secondary Name: The Great Hymn to the Aten
Note: The Great Hymn to the Aten names Nefertiti at its conclusion as Akhenaten's beloved Great Royal Wife and Lady of the Two Lands.
Wenamun undertakes his journey as an emissary of Amun to obtain timber for the god's sacred barque, making Amun's temple authority central to the narrative.
The Instruction of Ptahhotep repeatedly presents right conduct, truthful speech, and competent service as the practice of maat within court and society.
The Eloquent Peasant makes maat—the demand for justice, balance, and right judgment—the central standard by which official power is tested.
The Instruction of Amenemope develops a late wisdom ethic of restraint, fairness, and trust in divine order that is repeatedly expressed through the language of maat.
The Decree of Horemheb presents royal reform as the correction of official abuse and the restoration of lawful order, a political application of the broader principle of maat.
The Shabaka Stone recounts the dispute between Horus and Seth and the settlement that establishes Horus as the legitimate heir of Osiris.
The Shabaka Stone places Isis within the Osirian succession narrative as Horus's mother and protector during the settlement of kingship.

The Teaching of King Amenemhat I and the Tale of Sinuhe share the dynastic crisis created by Amenemhat I's death: one speaks as the murdered king to his successor, while the other begins with an official's flight after hearing the news.
The Moscow and Rhind mathematical papyri are the two major surviving collections of Egyptian mathematical problems and preserve related scribal procedures in arithmetic and geometry.

The Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri are complementary New Kingdom witnesses to older Egyptian medicine: one emphasizes trauma and examination, while the other preserves extensive remedies and medical-magical treatments.
The Stela of Kamose and the Poem of Pentaur turn warfare against foreign powers into royal self-presentation, divine legitimation, and a claim that the king personally restored Egyptian strength.
The Stela of Kamose and the Victory Stela of Merneptah are monumental victory texts that frame military success as the restoration of order under a divinely favored king.

Primary Name: Satire of the Trades (Teaching of Dua-Khety)
Note: The Satire of the Trades and the Instruction of Amenemope belong to scribal education and wisdom culture: the former promotes the scribal profession, while the latter trains disciplined conduct and speech.
The Deir el-Medina Strike Papyrus and the Harem Conspiracy Papyrus are rare Ramesside administrative records that expose institutional conflict from below and within the royal court respectively.
The Book of Amduat and the Litany of Re are closely related New Kingdom royal funerary works: one maps Re's night journey, while the other names the many forms through which the sun-god is renewed.
